html:
The Republic of Venice was a trading state built on islands in a lagoon at the head of the Adriatic Sea, which lasted from its legendary founding in 697 until Napoleon ended it in 1797. For much of that time it was one of the great naval and commercial powers of Europe.

The first doge, said to have been elected in 697, is a legend. In fact Venice began as a far outpost of the Eastern Roman Empire and drifted into independence during the 800s. Its link to Constantinople was its fortune: the Golden Bull of 1082 gave its merchants free trade across the Byzantine lands.

How it grew:

  • In 1204 Venice steered the Fourth Crusade to sack Constantinople and took Crete, islands and a share of the city.
  • Its galleys carried spices, silk and cotton from the Levant to Europe; the state ran convoys and built ships at its Arsenal.
  • It beat its rival Genoa in the War of Chioggia (1378 to 1381), opening the age the chart calls Venice at the centre.
  • In the 1400s it took a mainland empire in northern Italy.

Government was a closed aristocracy. An elected doge served for life but was boxed in by councils drawn from a fixed list of noble families, and the system stayed stable for centuries.

Decline was slow. The Ottomans took its eastern colonies one by one, and the Portuguese sea route to India after Vasco da Gama bypassed its spice trade. Venice ended as a city of art and pleasure, painted by Canaletto, until Napoleon handed it to Austria.
